notes.b: A performance analysis is only useful if it changes what you do next. The weaknesses it finds become the goals of your plan, so every goal has evidence behind it.
points: The main areas for development identified in the analysis become the performance goals, with one goal written for each area. In the project these are four areas, so there are four goals.
Each goal is linked to its evidence: the analysis result that revealed the weakness becomes the reason for the goal, which shows the goal was chosen for a reason and not by guesswork.
Example: an observation checklist (a list of technique points ticked off while watching) showing the elbow flaring out during the shot gives a technical goal about elbow position.
Priorities are set by how much each weakness limits performance in the activity, so the weakness costing most performance is addressed first.
Goals are linked to the demands of the activity (what the activity requires of a performer), so that improvements transfer to competition.
notes.tip: When asked how analysis informed planning, name the specific result from your analysis and then the goal it produced. Do not just say the analysis 'helped'.

notes.b: Not all goals are the same kind. They differ in how much of the result is in your own hands, and that decides which kind is most useful in training.
points: Outcome goals concern results, such as winning a league. They also depend on opponents and conditions, so you can do everything right and still miss them.
Performance goals set a personal standard that is independent of others, such as raising free-throw success from 60% to 75% (illustrative figures). Another team's play cannot stop you reaching it.
Process goals concern technique or behaviour that the performer controls, such as keeping the elbow under the ball when shooting.
Most short-term goals are performance or process goals, because the performer controls them more directly than outcomes.
notes.tip: Give an example for each type, and label any figures in a performance goal as illustrative. Examiners can ask you to define a performance goal.

notes.b: Big aims are reached by small steps. Splitting goals by time lets you check progress along the way instead of waiting until the end.
points: Short-term goals are achieved in a few days to a few weeks and are broken into steps.
Long-term goals are achieved over a season or more and are usually built from several short-term goals.
Each short-term step leads towards the long-term goal, so the achievement of one step is checked before the next is set.
notes.tip: A common question asks you to define a short-term goal. Say it is achieved in a few days to a few weeks, then give an example.

notes.b: A vague goal such as 'get better at shooting' cannot be checked. SMART is a five-letter test that turns an aim into a goal you can plan for and judge.
points: Specific: the goal states exactly what will improve, so you know what to practise.
Measurable: a number or test result shows whether the goal has been achieved.
Achievable: the goal is a stretch that the performer can reach with effort and the planned training, so it is neither too easy nor out of reach.
Realistic: the goal is possible given the time, facilities and circumstances available, such as how many weeks and what equipment you have.
Time-bound: the goal has a deadline or review date, which stops it drifting.

Example short-term performance goal: by the next competition, raise free-throw success in training from the baseline recorded in the first analysis to 75% (illustrative figure), measured out of a set number of attempts in each session.
notes.tip: When asked to write a short-term performance goal, include a skill, a starting figure, a target figure, a way of measuring and a deadline. That covers all five letters.

notes.h: Designing the practice or training plan
notes.b: Once goals are set, the plan says how you will reach them. A good plan matches the method to each goal and each choice can be justified from theory.
points: Plan contents: the goals; the methods and drills for each goal; the sessions per week, their duration and how they progress across the weeks.

Each goal has matched methods: skill practice for a technique goal, fitness training for an endurance goal and psychological strategies for a concentration goal, because each method trains a different quality.
Each session includes a warm-up (to prepare the body) and cool-down (to help recovery), and the plan sets the rest days and how progress will be recorded.
FITT (frequency, intensity, time, type) is applied to each component of training, using guidance values for each component.
Each design choice is linked to a principle of training or effective practice, such as progression in the weekly load or variety in the drills.
Distributed practice (shorter sessions with rest between) suits a beginner, because rest between shorter sessions lowers fatigue and injury risk.
Progressive overload (gradually increasing the training load) suits a strength goal, because the load is raised as the performer adapts, so strength keeps improving.
Sessions per week are justified by the principles of recovery: the plan must allow enough rest for adaptation (the body getting stronger after training) to take place.
notes.tip: Never just list what you did. Give each choice a reason from theory, for example distributed practice for a beginner or progressive overload for strength.

notes.b: A plan is not fixed once written. Evidence collected during the programme shows whether it is working, and reflection turns that evidence into changes.
points: Training logs or diaries record each session's content, load and how it felt to the performer.
Video of the performance is recorded at intervals and checked against the same checklist used in the analysis, so changes in technique can be seen.
Mid-programme retests repeat some of the analysis tests partway through the programme to check progress.
Heart-rate data show whether training intensity stayed at the intended level.
Coach feedback is recorded alongside the performer's own notes, giving an outside view as well as your own.
Reflection asks what went well, what did not, why it happened and what to change next.
Adapting: increase the difficulty when a target is reached early, so training keeps challenging you.
Adapting: change a drill that is not improving the goal, and adjust the load or the exercises when an injury limits training.
notes.tip: Exams often ask how progress was evidenced. Name specific sources, such as logs, video at intervals, mid-programme retests, heart-rate data and coach feedback, and say what each showed.

notes.h: Concluding analysis and evidence of effectiveness
notes.b: At the end you repeat the analysis to find out whether the plan worked. The evidence must be fair and tied back to each goal.
points: Repeat the same methods of analysis used at the start, under the same conditions, so that results can be compared fairly.
Before-and-after test scores show change in the fitness components measured at the start.
Success rates, video comparison and notational statistics (counts of events recorded during play) show change in skill, technique and tactics.
For each goal, state whether it was achieved, partly achieved or not achieved, and give the reason from the evidence.
A goal may be missed because a drill was unsuitable, practice was insufficient, an injury interrupted training or the goal was set too high.
Each result is linked back to the goal and the method designed to produce it, so the evidence shows whether the plan worked.
Next steps: new goals for continued improvement are set from the concluding analysis, and the cycle begins again.
notes.tip: For each goal say achieved, partly achieved or not achieved, and always give the reason, backed by before-and-after evidence.

notes.h: How the cycle is assessed in the Physical Activity Project
notes.b: The planning cycle you have just met is the structure of the Physical Activity Project, so knowing it helps both the project and written questions about it.
points: The Physical Activity Project is worth 20% of the overall mark.
It follows this cycle over eight to ten weeks, in the role of performer or coach/choreographer.
The specification describes four sections: performance analysis; identification of four performance goals; evidence of ongoing training or practice and reflection; and concluding analysis.
Reflection is written in alongside the ongoing evidence and the concluding analysis, rather than as a separate section.
The SEC sets the booklet layout and how many goals and plans are needed, so follow the current year's booklet rather than older guidance.
Written-exam questions may describe a planning cycle carried out during the course and ask about its stages.
notes.tip: Questions are often framed as 'as part of your studies you designed...'. Answer from your own cycle: how analysis informed the plan, then how progress was evidenced.

keyTerms.definition: A personal standard of performance that is independent of others, such as a measurable improvement in a skill.
A goal based on the result of a competition, which depends partly on opponents and conditions.
A goal about technique or behaviour that the performer controls.
A goal achieved within days or weeks and broken into steps.
A goal achieved over a season or more, usually built from short-term goals.
A goal that is specific, measurable, achievable, realistic and time-bound.
The starting measurement from the initial analysis, against which progress is judged.
A written record of each session's content, load and how it felt to the performer.
A repeat of some analysis tests partway through a programme to check progress.
Deciding whether each goal was achieved, partly achieved or not achieved, and why.
Changing the training plan in response to monitoring evidence and reflection.
Measured results linked back to the goals and methods, showing whether the plan worked.

questions.prompt: Define a short-term goal and a performance goal, and write a short-term performance goal for a physical activity of your choice.
questions.model: A short-term goal is achieved within a few days or weeks and is broken into steps. A performance goal is a personal standard of performance that is independent of other performers. Activity: basketball. Short-term performance goal: by the next competition, raise free-throw success in training from the baseline recorded in the first analysis to 75% (illustrative figure), measured out of a set number of attempts in each session. The goal is specific to the free throw, measurable through the success rate, achievable with the planned drills, realistic for the training time available, and time-bound by the competition date.

questions.prompt: Explain how information from a performance analysis can be used to plan for optimum performance, and how the effectiveness of the plan can be evidenced.
questions.model: Activity: basketball. The initial analysis used a technique checklist and video, which showed the elbow flaring out and the release point varying; a success rate out of a set number of attempts, which fell under pressure; a fitness test battery, which showed endurance fading late in games; and notational counts, which showed the player shooting when a team-mate was better placed. The four areas for development are therefore technical (the shooting action), fitness (endurance), tactical (shot selection) and psychological (concentration under pressure). Each becomes a performance goal: a process goal to keep the elbow under the ball, a performance goal to raise success under pressure, a fitness goal to hold shooting accuracy late in games, and a tactical goal to pass when a team-mate is better placed. The plan matches methods to goals: fixed practice for the shooting action, a conditioned endurance routine for fitness, pressure drills for concentration, and variable practice with defenders for shot selection, with the load progressed week by week. Progress is monitored with a training log, video recorded at intervals and checked against the same checklist, and a mid-programme retest; the plan is adapted when a drill stops improving its goal. At the end the same methods are repeated under the same conditions: the checklist, the success rate, the fitness battery and the notational counts of shot selection. Each goal is judged achieved, partly achieved or not achieved from the before-and-after results, so the effectiveness of the programme is shown.
